metaDescription: Six benchtop jointers, 6 and 8 inch, spiral and straight cutterheads, compared on table length, fence, dust collection and the flat-board limits.
expertTake: The WEN JT833H with its 8 inch width, spiral cutterhead and extendable tables is the best pick for a small shop that wants to flatten wider stock. The Cutech 40160HB is the value pick for narrow stock and edge jointing. A benchtop jointer will not give you flat long boards, so anyone milling rough lumber regularly should look at a floor-standing jointer.
introParagraphs: A jointer flattens one face of a board and squares one edge, which is the first step in turning rough lumber into accurate stock. A benchtop version does the same job in a smaller, lighter and cheaper machine, and it is popular with hobbyists who have limited space.

The tradeoff is table length. A short bed cannot reference a long, bowed board as well as a floor model, so benchtop jointers are best for short stock, edge jointing and small projects. Cutterhead style and fence quality decide how good the results are.

products.name: WEN JT833H 8 in Spiral Benchtop Jointer, Extendable Table
products.description:
The JT833H is the widest, longest-bedded jointer in the group. It cuts 8 inches wide, has a 33 by 8 inch table with support arms that extend to 51 inches, and uses a spiral cutterhead with 16 staggered HSS blades. The extendable table is the standout, because table length is the main weakness of a benchtop machine.

A spiral cutterhead shears the wood at an angle instead of chopping straight across, which reduces tear-out on figured grain and runs quieter than straight knives. This one uses staggered HSS blades rather than carbide inserts, so they dull faster and cannot be rotated like inserts. Compared with the Cutech 40180HI, the WEN has the longer extendable table, while the Cutech has cast iron tables and carbide inserts.

A 10 amp motor is adequate for light cuts in hardwood, and the dust port needs a dust collector. Expect to set the tables coplanar when you get it, and keep the fence square. It is the best choice if you want width and length on a bench. A short-bed machine rewards a simple routine: joint one face, then one edge against the fence, then plane to thickness on a separate planer.
products.bestFor: Small shops that want 8 in width and a longer bed on a benchtop machine.
pros: Spiral head is quieter than straight knives
cons: HSS blades dull faster than carbide inserts
10 amp motor limits cut depth in hardwood

products.name: Cutech 40180HI 8 in Spiral Jointer, Cast Iron Tables
products.description:
The Cutech 40180HI pairs an 8 inch spiral cutterhead with cast iron tables and a long 24 inch aluminum fence. The cutterhead holds 16 two-sided tungsten carbide inserts in six staggered rows, so you can rotate or flip a dull insert instead of resharpening a knife.

Cast iron tables stay flatter and heavier than aluminum ones, which helps the machine reference a board accurately, and the long fence supports wide edges. Carbide inserts outlast HSS and cost less to maintain over years. Compared with the WEN JT833H, the Cutech has better tables and cutters but a shorter bed without extension.

Cast iron means more weight, so it is less portable. Expect to adjust table height and coplanarity and to replace inserts with the proper torx screws. It is a solid choice for a serious hobbyist. Replacing blades one at a time keeps the head balanced, and torquing the screws to the maker's spec prevents inserts shifting.
products.bestFor: Hobbyists who want cast iron tables and carbide inserts at 8 in width.

products.name: Cutech 40160HB 6 in Spiral Jointer, 12 TC Inserts
products.description:
The Cutech 40160HB is the 6 inch member of the family, with a spiral cutterhead holding 12 carbide inserts, teflon-coated aluminum tables and a 19-5/8 inch bed. Teflon coating reduces friction so boards glide over the tables.

A 6 inch spiral head with carbide inserts at this price tier is an attractive combination: it cuts smoothly and the inserts last. The bed length is the weakness, at about 20 inches, which means it works best on short boards and edges. Compared with the straight-knife VEVOR 6 inch, it has a quieter spiral head, and compared with its 8 inch sibling it has a smaller, lighter body.

For small stock, edge jointing and shop jigs it is a good machine. Keep the tables clean and waxed, and use push blocks. It suits a hobbyist with limited space. On a bench it needs to be clamped or bolted down, because the force of a deep cut can walk a light machine across the top.
products.bestFor: Hobbyists who joint short boards and edges and want a spiral head at a low price.
cons: Aluminum tables flex more than cast iron

products.name: WEN JT630H 6 in Spiral Benchtop Jointer, 30 in Table
products.description:
The JT630H has a 6 inch width and a 30 by 6 inch table, noticeably longer than the Cutech 6 inch at about 20 inches. It uses a spiral cutterhead with 12 staggered HSS blades and a 10 amp motor.

A longer bed helps a short machine reference a bowed board, and 30 inches is respectable for a benchtop. The HSS blades give a good finish when sharp but need replacing sooner than carbide inserts. Compared with the Cutech 40160HB, it has more bed and less cutter life.

The 6 inch width limits you to narrow stock, so wide panel faces are out of reach. Check the knife height and table alignment on arrival. It suits a hobbyist who joints boards up to 6 inches and values bed length. Fit the extension arms before the first cut and check that they stay level when loaded with a long board.
products.bestFor: Small shops that need a longer bed on a 6 in machine.
pros: 30 in table is long for 6 in class
cons: HSS blades dull sooner than carbide

products.name: CRAFTSMAN CMEW020 Benchtop Jointer, 22,000 CPM
products.description:
The CRAFTSMAN CMEW020 uses a two-knife straight cutterhead with jackscrew knife leveling, a variable speed range of 6,000 to 11,000 RPM and up to 22,000 cuts per minute. Variable speed lets you slow the cutter for hard or dense wood.

Straight knives give a very smooth surface when sharp, but they are noisier and more prone to tear-out in figured grain than spiral heads. Jackscrews make it easier to set knife height, a job that is otherwise a chore. Compared with the WEN spiral units, it has simpler cutters and brand support.

Knives need sharpening or replacement, and you will need to set them level with the outfeed table. It is a good choice for someone who knows how to set knives and wants a recognised brand. Variable speed matters less than sharp knives, so spend a little on a spare set before anything else.
products.bestFor: Woodworkers who want a brand-name machine and are comfortable setting knives.
cons: Straight knives tear out figured grain more

products.name: VEVOR 6 in Benchtop Jointer 2HP 12,000 RPM Straight Head
products.description:
The VEVOR is the lowest-priced machine here by priceTier, a 6 inch jointer with a 2 HP rated motor, 12,000 RPM, a two-blade straight cutterhead and a 6 by 23 inch table. The 2 HP label is a peak figure, so the real power is closer to a 10 amp motor.

A 23 inch bed is slightly longer than the Cutech 6 inch and shorter than the WEN JT630H. Two HSS blades are simple to replace but leave a less smooth finish than spiral heads and are noisier. Compared with the CRAFTSMAN, it has no brand support but a lower price.

Set the blades level with the outfeed table and check the fence for square. It suits a hobbyist who wants the cheapest way to joint edges. Because the head is fast, always use push blocks and keep your hands clear of the cutter.
products.bestFor: Budget shoppers who joint narrow stock and accept a straight-knife head.
pros: Lowest price tier in the lineup
cons: Straight head tears out figured grain

buyingCriteria.explanation: A straight head holds two or three knives that chop across the board and need frequent sharpening and careful height setting. A spiral head holds many small carbide inserts or staggered blades, shears the grain and runs quieter. The WEN JT630H and JT833H use staggered HSS blades, while the Cutech models use carbide inserts you can rotate. Spiral is better on figured wood. On a short bed, take light passes and keep pressure on the outfeed side after the board passes the head, which is how you keep the face flat.

A longer bed supports the board and helps flatten a bowed face. The WEN JT833H extends to 51 inches, the JT630H runs 30 inches and the Cutech 40160HB only about 20 inches. For boards longer than about three feet, a short bed will not give a reliably flat face. Inserts cost a few dollars each in a pack, which is far cheaper over time than regrinding straight knives.

Cast iron, as on the Cutech 40180HI, stays flat and absorbs vibration but adds weight. Aluminum, as on the Cutech 40160HB, is light but can flex. A jointer is a precision tool, so table flatness and coplanarity matter more than motor amps. Check table flatness with a straightedge before the first cut, because a dished table is not always visible.

The fence must stay square to the table and lock firmly. A tilting fence from 90 to 135 degrees is useful for bevels. A short or flexing fence will give a crooked edge no matter how good the cutter is. Check it with a square on arrival. If the fence is not square, shim it or return the machine, since you cannot joint a square edge against a crooked fence.

Six inches suits edge jointing and narrow stock. Eight inches gives you width for wider boards. Most benchtop jointers cut up to 1/8 inch per pass, and light passes give a better finish. Do not expect to joint heavy hardwood in a single deep cut. Light cuts of about 1/16 inch leave a better surface than a single deep pass and reduce the load on a small motor.

A jointer throws a lot of chips, and a benchtop unit's small dust port clogs easily. Plan on a dust collector or a shop vacuum with a cyclone separator. Without it the machine will clog and overheat. A shop vacuum on the port plus a chip deflector is a minimum, and a dust collector is better.

howWeEvaluated.title: Cutterhead design
howWeEvaluated.description: We compared spiral heads with carbide inserts, spiral heads with staggered HSS blades and straight knives, because the cutterhead drives finish quality and upkeep. Bed length was weighed against stock length.

howWeEvaluated.title: Bed length and tables
howWeEvaluated.description: We compared bed length, from about 20 inches on the Cutech 40160HB to 51 inches on the extended WEN JT833H, and noted table materials. Carbide inserts were credited for lower upkeep.

howWeEvaluated.title: Width and power
howWeEvaluated.description: We looked at cutting width, 6 or 8 inches, and motor amps. Table material was treated as a flatness indicator.

howWeEvaluated.title: Fence and adjustability
howWeEvaluated.description: We noted fence length and tilt range. Fence length and tilt were noted.

cards.label: Spiral
cards.text: The Cutech and WEN models shear the grain, tear out less and run quieter. Carbide inserts rotate to a fresh edge.

cards.label: Straight
cards.text: The CRAFTSMAN and VEVOR use two knives. They are simpler and cheaper but louder and harder to set.

howToChoose.note: Choose spiral for figured hardwoods and straight knives only if budget or brand matters more.

cards.label: Look for
cards.text: A smooth cutterhead, a square fence and a dust port. For small parts, 6 inch width and a shorter bed are fine.

cards.label: In this comparison
cards.text: The Cutech 40160HB suits small stock, and the WEN JT630H gives a little more bed if you move to longer parts.

cards.label: Spend more if
cards.text: You joint wide or figured boards regularly. The WEN JT833H or Cutech 40180HI justifies it.

cards.label: Save if
cards.text: You joint edges on small projects. The Cutech 40160HB or VEVOR is enough.

maintenance.why: The outfeed table must be level with the knife at top dead centre. Misalignment causes snipe or a taper. Use a machinist's straightedge.
Dull edges burn and tear out. Rotate inserts or replace HSS blades. Use the right torx driver.
Pitch and rust slow the board. Paste wax keeps it gliding. Use paste wax, not oil.
A clogged port overheats the motor and blows chips onto the tables. Do it before the chips build up.
A fence out of square gives a crooked edge. Use a combination square.

faq.q: Can a benchtop jointer flatten a long board?
faq.a: Not reliably. A short bed cannot reference a bowed board longer than its tables. For long boards use a floor jointer or a planer sled. A jointer and a planer work as a pair.

The VEVOR and Cutech 40160HB sit at the low end, the WEN and CRAFTSMAN in the middle and the Cutech 40180HI at the top. Pay more for cast iron and carbide inserts. Prices vary, so compare on the day you buy.

faq.q: How long do jointer knives last?
faq.a: HSS knives dull in a few weeks of heavy use, while carbide inserts last much longer and can be rotated. Dull cutters burn wood and tear out. Keep spare cutters for your machine.

faq.q: Is a spiral head worth it?
faq.a: For figured and hard woods, yes. It reduces tear-out and noise. Straight knives are cheaper but less forgiving. A planer sled can flatten wide boards without a jointer.

faq.q: Do I need a dust collector?
faq.a: Yes. A jointer produces a lot of chips, and a small port clogs quickly. A shop vacuum is the minimum. Dust collection also keeps the tables clean.
Only with push blocks and careful technique. Never joint a board shorter than about 12 inches by hand. Always use push blocks.
